questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a census enumerates everyone
questions.stem: A trainee suggests using a sample instead of a census for a national count. Why is full enumeration preferred?

options.text: A census aims to count every resident, not just estimate from a subset.
Sampling is always cheaper, so it is never used.
Censuses only count citizens, not all residents.
Sampling guarantees exact counts every time.

questions.explanation: A census enumerates the entire population to provide a complete count. Sampling estimates from a subset and is useful for other purposes, but it does not replace full enumeration for a census.

questions.explanation: Demographic change over ten years can alter age structures and totals. Planning with an outdated census risks mismatched services and wasted capacity.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Checking a census against a survey

stimulus.body: A census counts 100,000 residents in a district, while a recent survey estimates 108,000.

questions.stem: What is the most likely reason for the difference?

options.text: The census must be wrong because surveys are newer.
Surveys estimate and can differ from an exact census count.
The two figures measure completely different populations.
Censuses always overcount, so 100,000 is too high.

questions.explanation: A census aims for a complete count, while a survey estimates from a sample and can differ. Neither is automatically wrong; the gap reflects method and timing differences.

questions.stem: A city had 500,000 residents, saw 20,000 births, 15,000 deaths, 8,000 in-migrants, and 12,000 out-migrants. What is the new population?
questions.explanation: Start with 500,000, add natural increase of 5,000, then add net migration of -4,000. The result is 501,000. Forgetting net migration gives 505,000.

questions.topic: Choosing a denominator for a migration rate

questions.stem: A trainee computes a migration rate using total population as the denominator. What is the usual issue?

options.text: Migration rates never use population denominators.
options.misconception: denies the use of population denominators

options.text: Any denominator gives the same rate, so it does not matter.
Migration rates often use the population at risk or midyear population, not an arbitrary total.
Only the number of migrants should be reported.

questions.explanation: A migration rate standardizes flows by a relevant population, often the population at risk or midyear population. Using an arbitrary total can distort the rate and make comparisons invalid.
questions.hint: Match denominator to the at-risk population.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Compute net migration in a balance
questions.stem: A city population balance shows 400,000 start, 12,000 births, 9,000 deaths, and a final population of 405,000. What is net migration?
questions.explanation: Natural increase is 3,000. Final minus start minus natural increase equals net migration: 405,000 minus 400,000 minus 3,000 equals 2,000. Ignoring natural change would give 5,000.
questions.hint: Final minus start minus natural increase.

questions.stem: A district had 600 net migrants and a midyear population of 120,000. What is the net migration rate per 1,000 residents?

questions.hint: Net migrants divided by midyear population, times 1,000.

questions.stem: A population pyramid has a narrow base. What does this most directly suggest?

options.text: The population is definitely growing rapidly.
options.misconception: reverses the implication of a narrow base

options.text: A smaller share of the population is young.
Fertility is extremely high.
options.misconception: confuses narrow base with high fertility

options.text: Migration is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: A narrow base indicates fewer young people. It does not prove rapid growth, high fertility, or irrelevance of migration; those need the full pyramid.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A report uses sampling for a quick household survey. Why is sampling acceptable here?

answer.exemplar: Sampling is acceptable for timely estimates between censuses, as long as its uncertainty is acknowledged and not treated as an exact count.

questions.explanation: Sampling provides timely estimates between censuses. It is acceptable when its uncertainty is acknowledged and not mistaken for an exact count.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A planner uses a 20-year-old census for current policy. What is the main risk?

options.text: Census year has no effect on planning.
Old census data is always more accurate.
Plans may reflect outdated population distribution and needs.
Censuses are useless for any policy.

questions.explanation: A 20-year-old census may not reflect current distribution and needs, leading to outdated plans. Census year matters because populations change.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Checking a census against a survey
questions.stem: A census and survey differ by 3%. Why might this occur?

answer.exemplar: Differences can arise from sampling error, different reference dates, or coverage gaps, so a small gap does not necessarily mean one source is wrong.

questions.explanation: A 3% gap can arise from sampling error, different reference dates, or coverage gaps. A small difference does not necessarily mean one source is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A city starts with 180,000 residents, has 5,000 births, 4,000 deaths, 2,000 in-migrants, and 3,000 out-migrants. What is the final population?
questions.explanation: Natural increase is 1,000 and net migration is -1,000, total change 0. Final population remains 180,000. Ignoring migration gives 181,000.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Choosing a denominator for a migration rate
questions.stem: A trainee computes an out-migration rate using the destination's population. What is wrong?

options.text: Only in-migration needs a denominator.
Destination population is always correct for out-migration.
No denominator is needed for out-migration.
Out-migration rates should use the origin population at risk, not the destination's.

questions.explanation: An out-migration rate should use the origin population at risk. Using the destination's population misaligns the rate with the population exposed to leaving.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how remittances affect village consumption
questions.stem: A report notes remittances raise village consumption. Why does this matter for local businesses?

answer.exemplar: Higher consumption increases demand for local goods and services, supporting village businesses and potentially creating jobs.

questions.explanation: Remittances raise household spending, which increases demand for local goods and services. This can support village businesses and create local jobs.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Remittances as a share of income
questions.stem: A household's total income is 15,000, with 3,000 from remittances. What share is remittances, in percent?
questions.explanation: Divide remittances by total income: 3,000 divided by 15,000 equals 0.20, or 20 percent. Using local income of 12,000 as the denominator gives 25 percent, which is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a pyramid's base cannot stand alone
questions.stem: A report reads a pyramid's base and top together. Why is this better than reading the base alone?

options.text: The top is irrelevant to population analysis.
It reveals both youth share and aging, giving a fuller growth picture.
Only the base ever matters.
Pyramids cannot show aging.

questions.explanation: Reading base and top together reveals both youth share and aging, giving a fuller picture of growth and future needs than the base alone.
questions.hint: Base plus top gives full picture.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A report uses census data to draw electoral boundaries. Why is a census suited to this?

options.text: Sampling is always better for boundaries.
Censuses are only for estimating, not counting.
It provides complete population counts for each area.
Boundaries do not need population data.

questions.explanation: Electoral boundaries need complete population counts for each area. A census provides these counts, making it well suited to the task.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Checking a census against a survey
questions.stem: A statistician uses a survey to update census figures between counts. Why is this useful?

options.text: Census data never becomes outdated.
Surveys replace the need for any future census.
Surveys are always more accurate than censuses.
Surveys provide timely interim estimates when no new census exists.

questions.explanation: Surveys provide timely interim estimates between censuses. They complement rather than replace full enumeration.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a population balance
questions.stem: A report uses a population balance to verify growth. Why is this valuable?

answer.exemplar: The balance checks whether births, deaths, and migration sum to observed growth, revealing data errors or unrecorded flows.

questions.explanation: A population balance checks whether births, deaths, and migration sum to observed growth. Mismatches reveal data errors or unrecorded flows.
